Q: Can I use `@overload` to fix this typing issue? A:

The problem is that @overload only helps type checkers determine which argument combinations are valid when some_func() is called. It doesn't make input_type act as a discriminator for the type of input inside the function body.

In other words, Pylance still sees input as:

ItemQueue | Callable[[Item], None] | Callable[[Item], Coroutine[Any, Any, None]]

regardless of which input_type branch you're in.

I would avoid Any here. Instead, I'd either explicitly narrow the type in each branch:

if input_type == InputType.QUEUE:
    assert isinstance(input, ItemQueue)
    func1(input)
elif input_type == InputType.CALLBACK:
    assert callable(input)
    input(item)
elif input_type == InputType.CORO:
    assert inspect.iscoroutinefunction(input)
    coro = input(item)
    asyncio.create_task(coro)

Or, preferably, I'd remove input_type altogether. The actual value already tells you what it is, so having a second argument describing its type means you now have two pieces of information that have to stay in sync.

For example:

def some_func(
    input: ItemQueue
    | Callable[[Item], None]
    | Callable[[Item], Coroutine[Any, Any, None]]
) -> None:
    item = Item("type", 1)

    if isinstance(input, ItemQueue):
        func1(input)
    elif inspect.iscoroutinefunction(input):
        asyncio.create_task(input(item))
    elif callable(input):
        input(item)
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"Unsupported input type: {type(input)!r}")

This also makes an invalid combination like some_func(queue, InputType.CORO) impossible in the first place, rather than something the function has to detect at runtime.

So I don't think Any is necessary here. The main thing I'd change is the API itself: let the type of input determine what should happen instead of passing that information separately.

Q: Is this C++ compatiblity header setup for new features unavailable in older C++ versions a good idea? A:

Would it be better to just #include the alternative header and have a using directive after the #include where ever it is used?

No. Because this will add the alternate header (e.g. zeus/expected.hpp) and increase the compilation time (and possibly the executable size) for builds that don't use it. Since you are compiling for embedded platforms, this is a downside worth considering.

As pointed in the comments, if you go with #if, see https://cppreference.com/cpp/feature_test for a better include switch selector.

Alternative from the comments:

using namespace compat = zeus; and using namespace compat = std; makes it easier and more generic.

It also makes it impossible to select individual features (classes). It's all or nothing, which is not good.

Of course, only 100% API compatible replacement libraries/headers should be used, otherwise things will break when compiled with a newer C++ standard.

Be careful with that. For instance, even when std::foo is promoted from tr1::foo and/or brought in from boost::foo, usually they differ in some API points. Some of those give compile errors, but some just silently change the behavior.

You will get better chances with user libraries designed with the goal of being API compatible with the std equivalent. But even then, bugs, or language features might create different APIs or behaviors.

It's a nice dream to be able to just replace using custom::foo; with using std::foo and have it all work out.

In practice, there is a non insignificant chance to find those edge cases where there is a difference and you have to work around it, or create more wrappers around them. Be prepared.

In any case, I strongly recommend creating comprehensive unit tests to protect yourself against surprizes.

Q: When it is best to apply Unique constraint? A:

A UNIQUE constraint depends on the business rules, not on the one-to-many relationship.

Usually, the subcategory name should be unique only inside its category: Example.

UNIQUE (category_id, english_name)

This prevents duplicate subcategories in the same category but allows the same name in different categories.

Use UNIQUE (english_name) only if the name must be unique across all categories.
